strengths: Provides a theoretical analysis of the Fisher information matrix (FIM) on the statistical simplex and derives deterministic lower/upper bounds that are then extended to classifier networks.
Proposes a Hutchinson-style unbiased FIM estimator that can be computed with a single additional backward pass via auto-differentiation and the detach trick.
Establishes variance bounds for the diagonal entries of the proposed estimator, showing a bounded coefficient of variation up to sqrt(2) under Rademacher probes.
The paper is generally well organized, with notation and proof steps separated into the main text and appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the core idea of using Hutchinson's trace estimator and score outer products for FIM estimation is largely a straightforward combination of existing techniques, and the specific detach-based implementation is incremental.

Evaluation is inadequate for a top-tier AI conference: only normalized density plots of diagonal FIM entries are shown for DistilBERT; there is no quantitative comparison to baselines, no ground-truth validation on small models, no downstream task, no empirical variance/bias study, and no code or detailed reproducibility information.

The claimed quality guarantee is over-stated: variance bounds are only derived for diagonal entries, while off-diagonal/full-tensor estimation is not analyzed and the variance for off-diagonal entries can be unbounded relative to the true value, especially when the true entry is near zero.

The proposed Hutchinson estimator is rank-1 per sample, so using it to estimate the full or block-diagonal FIM with a small number of samples remains impractical; the paper does not address this limitation convincingly.
The computational advantage is not fully realized for the lower-bound estimator, which still requires computing the top eigenpair for each data point via power iteration, with complexity O(M C |D|).

The deterministic bounds are not shown to be practically tight or useful in real settings; the upper bound can incur an error of at least 1/C even in the core space, and no empirical tightness comparison is provided.

No meaningful baselines or ablations are provided for estimator quality (e.g., eFIM, Monte Carlo FIM, KFAC-style approximations), making it difficult to assess the practical value of the proposed method.

strengths: Provides a clear information-geometric formulation of the Fisher information matrix (FIM) for classifier networks and connects it to a low-dimensional core statistical simplex.
Derives deterministic lower/upper bounds for the simplex FIM and extends them to neuromanifolds, with error analyses for empirical FIM and Monte Carlo estimators.
Proposes a simple Hutchinson-style unbiased estimator of the FIM that uses detached probabilities and can be computed with one additional backward pass.
Establishes variance bounds for diagonal FIM entries under Gaussian/Rademacher probes, giving a relative-error guarantee for the diagonal case.
The estimator is architecture-agnostic and can target diagonal, block-diagonal, or implicit full-FIM representations, which may be useful for large models.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core FIM spectrum and bounds largely follow from standard matrix perturbation/interlacing arguments, and the proposed estimator is a straightforward application of Hutchinson-type trace estimation / random feature-style sketching to the FIM.

Evaluation is far below top-tier AI conference standards: only qualitative density plots on DistilBERT are provided, with no downstream optimization experiments, no quantitative estimator-error metrics, no runtime/memory comparisons, and no comparison against established FIM approximations beyond eFIM.

The abstract overstates the guarantee: the bounded standard deviation result only covers diagonal entries, not the full metric tensor, off-diagonal entries, spectral norm, or matrix-level estimation quality. No matrix concentration bounds are given.

Several technical and notational issues appear: missing squares/typos in bounds (e.g., Lemma 3), ambiguous use of \hat{\mathcal F}, inconsistent \mathbb I / \mathbb F notation, a malformed Table 1, and proof steps that are either unclear or incorrect as written (e.g., inequalities involving tr(AB)^2 vs tr(A^2B^2)).

The claimed computational advantage is not rigorously established: the scalar h sums over all classes, and the backward pass may be more expensive than standard cross-entropy in some regimes; no empirical cost analysis is provided.

The theoretical bounds are often loose (e.g., the simplex upper bound incurs an error at least 1/C, and the eFIM worst-case bound can be pessimistic), limiting their practical significance without further empirical validation.
No code, reproducibility details, or ablation studies are provided, making it difficult to verify the estimator's practical behavior or claimed efficiency at scale.

The paper is positioned as a practical contribution for deep learning, but the experiments do not test any practical use case such as optimization, regularization, or natural-gradient training, so the significance remains largely theoretical and unvalidated.

strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of the Fisher information matrix on the simplex and extends it to neuromanifolds via pullback/Gauss-Newton structure, with deterministic lower and upper bounds and error estimates.

Introduces an unbiased Hutchinson-style random estimator for the FIM that can be computed with one additional backward pass using auto-differentiation and the detach trick, with bounded coefficient of variation for diagonal entries.
Analyzes relationships with empirical and Monte Carlo FIM estimators, showing cases where eFIM and MC estimators can have large or unbounded relative error.
Includes proofs for the main results in the appendix and qualitative numerical illustrations on DistilBERT for AG News and SST-2.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the core simplex spectral analysis largely applies known tools such as Cauchy interlacing, and the proposed Hutchinson-type estimator is conceptually close to existing stochastic trace/matrix estimators.

The empirical evaluation is limited to qualitative density plots; there is no quantitative validation of the deterministic bounds, variance behavior, or FIM approximation accuracy against computable metrics or baselines.

Claims about estimating the full tensor or block-diagonal tensor are stronger than the evidence: variance guarantees are established only for diagonal entries, and a rank-1 estimator may be severely rank-deficient in practice.
Several deterministic bounds are acknowledged to be loose, and the practical utility of the proposed bounds for optimization, uncertainty, or other downstream tasks is not demonstrated.
The paper leaves real applications and more thorough numerical experiments to future work, so its practical impact and competitiveness for a top-tier AI conference are not fully established.
Reproducibility details such as released code, runtime measurements, and detailed experimental protocols are missing.

strengths: The paper gives a rigorous and detailed theoretical analysis of the Fisher information matrix (FIM) on the probability simplex, including eigenvalue bounds and Löwner-order bounds, and extends these to deterministic bounds for classifier networks.

It proposes a practical Hutchinson-style unbiased FIM estimator that can be computed with a single backward pass via auto-differentiation, with a detach trick to avoid differentiating through the output probabilities.

Theoretical variance analysis is provided for the diagonal FIM estimator, showing bounded coefficient of variation under Rademacher probes, and the paper explains why Monte Carlo FIM can have unbounded variance.

The empirical study covers multiple architectures and modalities (DistilBERT, RoBERTa, ResNet, EfficientNet, Wav2Vec2; NLP, vision, audio) and compares several one-backward-pass estimators against ground-truth diagonal FIM, showing that the Hutchinson estimator is often more accurate and robust than the empirical FIM.
The paper carefully discusses failure modes of eFIM and provides error bounds for deterministic upper/lower bounds, which helps clarify the behavior of existing FIM approximations.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the simplex FIM formula is standard, the deterministic bounds follow from well-known matrix inequalities, and the Hutchinson-style estimator is a natural extension of existing randomized trace/Hessian estimation techniques to the FIM setting.

Evaluation is incomplete for a top-tier AI conference: only the diagonal FIM is tested, there are no error bars or variance studies across random probes/seeds, no Monte Carlo baseline, no K-FAC or other structured FIM comparisons, and no downstream application such as natural-gradient training or pruning.

The deterministic bounds are often loose and expensive to compute (spectral decompositions or power iterations), and their error bounds depend on spectral norms/order statistics that are not empirically validated at scale.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the estimator is called 'universal' and to have 'guaranteed quality,' but variance analysis and empirical validation are restricted to the diagonal, while full-tensor behavior is not demonstrated.

There are minor technical and presentation issues: e.g., a missing square in Lemma 3, ambiguous RelMAE formula/denominator, garbled table formatting, and the computational overhead of low-rank estimators is only partially quantified.

strengths: Provides rigorous closed-form spectral bounds for the simplex Fisher information matrix using Cauchy interlacing and Gershgorin-type arguments, which may be of independent interest.
Derives deterministic lower and upper bounds for the neuromanifold FIM via pullback from the core simplex, with Frobenius/spectral norm error analyses summarized in Propositions 5, 7, 8, 9, and 10.

Introduces a Hutchinson-style unbiased estimator for the FIM that can be computed with a single backward pass via auto-differentiation, with variance bounds for diagonal entries under Gaussian and Rademacher probes.

Includes an empirical study across several NLP, vision, and audio models (DistilBERT, RoBERTa, ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B0, Wav2Vec2) comparing empirical FIM and Hutchinson-based estimators on diagonal FIM entries.
Writing is mostly clear and the mathematical derivations are largely transparent and reproducible in principle.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the Hutchinson trick for estimating quadratic forms/matrices is standard, and its application to the FIM is a straightforward extension of existing trace-estimation and Monte Carlo FIM literature.

There is no downstream application or task-level evaluation (e.g., natural gradient training, pruning, transfer learning, or generalization), so the practical significance for deep learning remains unproven.

The empirical evaluation is narrow: it only assesses diagonal FIM entries on a fixed subset of 128 batches, with no full-matrix or inverse-FIM experiments and no comparison to important structured baselines such as K-FAC/EKFAC or Monte Carlo FIM under equal compute budgets.

The deterministic bound analysis is not empirically validated: the paper claims improved bound gaps/tightness but does not measure these quantities on real networks or compare them quantitatively to prior bounds such as Soen & Sun (2024).

Variance analysis and guarantees are limited to diagonal entries; the full metric tensor estimator is rank-1 with potentially enormous variance, yet the title and abstract discuss metric tensors broadly and the paper does not adequately analyze off-diagonal or full-matrix behavior.

The estimator relies on a non-differentiable detached probability vector to avoid bias; this implementation hack is not deeply justified or analyzed, and alternative formulations are relegated to an appendix with minimal comparison.

The empirical results include suspicious or underdiscussed numbers (e.g., RelMAE of 341 for F^DG on SST-2), and the RelMAE definition appears to contain a typo or inconsistency regarding the denominator.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release, incomplete implementation details for the power iteration and spectral decomposition, and no sensitivity analysis for probe count, batch size, or number of iterations.

Claims about advancing the state of the art in bound gap and variance are stronger than the evidence provided; the paper does not demonstrate clear superiority over existing FIM approximations in realistic settings.

The moving-average-over-learning-path idea for obtaining higher-rank estimates is mentioned but not tested, so the practical viability of the proposed estimator in large-scale settings remains speculative.

strengths: Introduces a practical unbiased estimator of the Fisher information matrix based on Hutchinson's trick, computable with a single backward pass and with bounded variance, which is useful for large-scale models.
Provides a clean theoretical path from the simplex core-space FIM to deterministic lower/upper bounds on the network FIM, with explicit error bounds and spectral analysis.

The empirical study spans multiple modalities (NLP, vision, audio) and modern architectures (DistilBERT, RoBERTa, ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B0, Wav2Vec2), showing consistent advantages of Hutchinson's estimate over the empirical FIM.
The paper is generally well written, with detailed proofs and appendices that support the main claims.
weaknesses: The Hutchinson estimator, while effective, is conceptually close to existing randomized trace/Hessian estimators; the novelty may be viewed as a straightforward adaptation to the FIM rather than a fundamental breakthrough.
The empirical evaluation focuses only on the diagonal FIM; the full metric tensor and off-diagonal structure are not evaluated, despite being a central object of the paper.
Baselines are limited mainly to the empirical FIM and variants of the proposed method; comparisons with other practical FIM approximations (e.g., K-FAC, structured low-rank methods) are missing.

The deterministic bounds are not directly evaluated on real networks as bound gaps; the experiments instead assess randomized estimators derived from those bounds, leaving the practical tightness of the deterministic envelopes underexplored.
There is no downstream application or optimizer built on the proposed estimator, so practical impact is somewhat speculative, as the authors acknowledge.

Some theoretical bounds rely on standard matrix inequalities and may be loose in practice, especially the upper bound; the paper could better quantify when the proposed bounds are preferable to existing bounds.
